subject: chemistry
title: Exothermic and endothermic reactions
key_idea: Energy is conserved in every reaction. An exothermic reaction transfers energy to the surroundings, so their temperature rises. An endothermic reaction takes in energy from the surroundings, so their temperature falls.

blocks.text: This section covers what exothermic and endothermic mean and where the energy goes.

items.meaning: A reaction that transfers energy to the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings increases.
A reaction that takes in energy from the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings decreases.
Everything around the reacting chemicals, such as the solution, the container and the air.

items: Energy is **conserved** in a chemical reaction. The amount of energy in the universe at the end is the same as before the reaction.
In an exothermic reaction, the energy transferred to the surroundings comes from the reacting chemicals.
So the product molecules have less energy than the reactants, by the amount transferred.
In an endothermic reaction, the products have more energy than the reactants, because energy is taken in from the surroundings.
Exothermic: energy goes out to the surroundings and the temperature rises.
Endothermic: energy is taken in from the surroundings and the temperature falls.

blocks.text: Learn which common reactions are exothermic and which are endothermic, and how each is used.

rows: Combustion, many oxidation reactions, neutralisation, displacement of a metal, calcium chloride dissolving in water
Thermal decomposition, citric acid reacting with sodium hydrogencarbonate, ammonium nitrate dissolving in water

diagram.alt: Sort reactions into exothermic and endothermic.
diagram.prompt: Sort each reaction or use into exothermic or endothermic.

items.text: Magnesium displacing copper from copper sulfate solution
Thermal decomposition of a metal carbonate
Citric acid reacting with sodium hydrogencarbonate

items: A cold pack goes cold when the solid inside dissolves in or reacts with water. The reaction takes in heat.
A cold pack can be used only once. The reaction cannot be reversed and the reactants are used up.
Choose the type of reaction to suit the job: exothermic to warm something, endothermic to cool it.
Combustion, oxidation and neutralisation are exothermic. Thermal decomposition is endothermic.
Hand warmers and self-heating cans use exothermic reactions. Sports injury packs use endothermic reactions.

sections.heading: Telling them apart from the temperature

blocks.text: You can classify a reaction from the temperature of its surroundings before and after. The sign of the change tells you the type.

blocks.label: Temperature change
blocks.formula: temperature change = final temperature − initial temperature
where: final temperature is the highest or lowest temperature reached, in °C
initial temperature is the starting temperature, in °C

items.text: A solution starts at 24.0 °C and falls to 19.5 °C. Change = 19.5 − 24.0 = −4.5 °C.
The sign is negative, so the temperature fell.
The surroundings lost energy to the reaction, so it is endothermic.

diagram.alt: Work out a temperature change with its sign.
diagram.question: A reaction mixture starts at {T1} °C and ends at {T2} °C. Work out the temperature change, including its sign.
working: Temperature change = final temperature − initial temperature
A positive value means exothermic. A negative value means endothermic.

items: Temperature change = final − initial, and the sign matters.
A rise is exothermic and a fall is endothermic.

checks.q: What happens to the temperature of the surroundings in an exothermic reaction, and why?
checks.a: It increases, because the reaction transfers energy to the surroundings.

checks.q: A reaction mixture starts at 21.0 °C and ends at 16.5 °C. Give the temperature change with its sign and state the type of reaction.
Give one everyday use of an exothermic reaction and one of an endothermic reaction.
checks.a: Exothermic: a hand warmer or self-heating can. Endothermic: a sports injury (cold) pack.

worked_example.question:
A student investigated the temperature change during the reaction between citric acid and sodium hydrogencarbonate solution. Citric acid is a solid.

The student poured 25 cm³ of sodium hydrogencarbonate solution into a polystyrene cup and measured its temperature. The student then added 0.25 g portions of citric acid, stirring and measuring the temperature each time.

Mass of citric acid added in g: 0.00, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.00, 1.25
Temperature of solution in °C: 22.6, 22.2, 21.8, 21.4, 21.0, 20.6

How do the results show that the reaction is endothermic?
answer_points: The temperature decreases during the reaction (the solution gets colder).
worked_example.tip: Use the temperature readings as the evidence. They fall from 22.6 °C to 20.6 °C.

worked_example.question:
A student poured 50 cm³ water into a beaker and measured the water's temperature.

The student added 1.00 g calcium chloride to the water, stirred the mixture and then recorded the temperature.

The student's results were
temperature of water at start = 21 °C
temperature of mixture after stirring = 32 °C

Explain, using these results, the type of heat energy change that occurs when calcium chloride dissolves in water.
answer_points: So it is an exothermic process (heat is given out to the surroundings).
worked_example.tip: One mark for the evidence and one for the type. Endothermic is rejected.

worked_example.question:
Phil investigates some exothermic and endothermic reactions. He measures the temperature changes during some chemical reactions.

Reaction A: start 15 °C, end 25 °C, change +10 °C
Reaction B: start 15 °C, end 15 °C, change 0 °C
Reaction C: start 18 °C, end 15 °C, change −3 °C
Reaction D: start 15 °C, end 20 °C, change +5 °C

What can you conclude about the type of energy change in each reaction? Explain your answer.
answer_points: A is exothermic as the temperature increases.
B is neither exothermic nor endothermic as the temperature stays the same.
C is endothermic as the temperature drops.
D is exothermic as the temperature increases.
worked_example.tip: One mark for each reaction. Give the type and the temperature evidence together.

worked_example.question:
Solid sodium hydrogencarbonate, NaHCO₃, reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid and with dilute ethanoic acid.

NaHCO₃(s) + HCl(aq) → NaCl(aq) + CO₂(g) + H₂O(l)
NaHCO₃(s) + CH₃COOH(aq) → CH₃COONa(aq) + CO₂(g) + H₂O(l)

These two reactions are endothermic.

Plan an investigation to find which of the two reactions is the most endothermic. Your plan must include how you can use the results to find which reaction is the most endothermic.

You are provided with solid sodium hydrogencarbonate, dilute hydrochloric acid, dilute ethanoic acid and common laboratory apparatus.
answer_points: Use a known mass of sodium hydrogencarbonate each time.
Use a known volume (and concentration) of each acid.
Name a suitable container, such as a polystyrene cup, and a way to measure the acid volume, such as a measuring cylinder.
Measure the temperature of the acid before mixing.
Add the reagents together and stir.
Measure the temperature of the mixture after the reaction.
The reaction with the biggest temperature decrease is the most endothermic.
worked_example.tip: Keep everything the same except the acid, so that the temperature falls can be compared fairly. Any six points score the marks.

blocks.text: (Supplement) The energy transferred in a reaction is the **enthalpy change**, ΔH.

items: (Supplement) ΔH is negative for an exothermic reaction, such as ΔH = −92 kJ/mol.
(Supplement) ΔH is positive for an endothermic reaction.

worked_example.question:
A student dissolves hydrated copper(II) sulfate in water.

initial temperature = 23.8 °C
final temperature when all the solid dissolves = 22.7 °C

Explain what the results show about the type of energy change that occurs when hydrated copper(II) sulfate dissolves.
answer_points: So the energy change is endothermic.
worked_example.tip: One mark for the evidence and one for the type.

items: Heating a metal carbonate decomposes it into a metal oxide and carbon dioxide.
For example, green copper(II) carbonate turns into black copper(II) oxide: CuCO₃ → CuO + CO₂.
